statement: In adults aged 18 or older living in US households and some group homes, a national face-to-face survey in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III; 36,309 people, 60.1% response; Grant et al., 2015; funded by the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, which also ran the survey, and the National Institute on Drug Abuse; no conflicts declared) found DSM-5 alcohol use disorder, diagnosed with a structured interview given by lay interviewers, in 13.9 in 100 adults in the past year (SE 0.31) and in 29.1 in 100 at some time in their lives. About half of the past-year cases were mild (7.3 in 100 adults mild, 3.2 moderate, 3.4 severe). The disorder was more common in men than in women (17.6 against 10.4 in 100 in the past year) and at ages 18 to 29 (26.7 in 100) than at 65 or older (2.3 in 100). Among adults who had drunk alcohol in the past year, 17.5 in 100 (95% CI 16.7 to 18.3) met the older DSM-IV criteria in the same survey, as did 54.5 in 100 of those who had drunk heavily at least once a week (4 or more US standard drinks of 14 g of alcohol in a day for women, 5 or more for men) (Grant et al., 2017). The figures depend on the survey: another national survey, cited by the same authors, found 7.0 in 100 adults with the disorder in the past year in 2013, about half the NESARC-III figure, and the authors do not explain the difference. NESARC-III left out homeless people, people in prison and most people in treatment, which the authors say may lower its figures, and 4 in 10 of the people sampled did not take part. By the older DSM-IV definition, the same institute's surveys found 8.5 in 100 adults with the disorder in 2001–2002 and 12.7 in 100 in 2012–2013, but the two surveys differed in design and response (81.0% against about 60%) and the other national survey showed a stable figure of about 7.5 in 100 over 2002 to 2013, so these studies cannot show whether the disorder became more common. For the world, a narrative review relays WHO estimates for 2016 of 5.1 in 100 people aged 15 or older (8.6 in 100 men, 1.7 in 100 women), which its authors call rough estimates; these figures are second-hand (Carvalho et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: In a large US survey in 2012–2013, about 14 in 100 adults had alcohol use disorder in the past year, about half of them in a mild form, and about 29 in 100 had had it at some time in their lives. It was most common in young adults and in men. Among adults who drank that year, about 18 in 100 met the older (DSM-IV) criteria. Another US survey found about half as many people with the disorder, so the number depends on how it is measured, and the survey left out people who were homeless, in prison or in treatment. A review passes on world estimates of about 5 in 100 people aged 15 or older in 2016. Whether the disorder became more common in the US between 2001 and 2013 cannot be told from these surveys.
population: Adults aged 18 or older in US households and selected group quarters (not homeless people, people in prison or most people in treatment), interviewed in 2012–2013 (NESARC-III, 36,309 people) and in 2001–2002 (NESARC, 43,093 people); the world population aged 15 or older in 2016 (WHO estimates, relayed second-hand)
exposure: Not applicable (prevalence); subgroups by sex and age, and past-year drinking and weekly heavy drinking as the denominators of the prevalence among people who drink
comparator: None for the prevalence; another US national survey (the National Survey on Drug Use and Health) as the authors report it; the 2001–2002 survey for the DSM-IV figures
outcome: Past-year (12-month) and lifetime DSM-5 alcohol use disorder by the AUDADIS-5 interview, by severity (mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe 6 or more of 11 criteria); past-year DSM-IV alcohol use disorder (abuse or dependence) overall, among people who drank and among people who drank heavily every week; WHO's 2016 prevalence of alcohol use disorders (case definition not stated in the review)
magnitude: Grant et al. 2015 (NESARC-III, weighted, % (SE)): past-year DSM-5 AUD 13.9 (0.31): mild 7.3 (0.19), moderate 3.2 (0.13), severe 3.4 (0.12); lifetime 29.1 (0.48): mild 8.6, moderate 6.6, severe 13.9; past year men 17.6, women 10.4; ages 18–29 26.7, 30–44 16.2, 45–64 10.0, 65 or older 2.3; lifetime men 36.0, women 22.7. Response 60.1% (screener 72.0%, person 84.0%). National Survey on Drug Use and Health, as cited: past-year AUD 7.0% in 2013, about 7.5% and stable over 2002–2013. Grant et al. 2017 (DSM-IV, past year, % (95% CI)): 2001–2002 8.5 (8.0–8.9), 2012–2013 12.7 (12.1–13.3), a difference of 4.2 percentage points (editors' calculation; the paper gives only the relative change, 49.4%); among people who drank in the past year 12.9 (interval printed as 12.3–17.5, a misprint) and 17.5 (16.7–18.3); among people who drank heavily at least weekly 46.5 (44.3–48.7) and 54.5 (52.7–56.4); response 81.0% (2001–2002) and 60.0% (2012–2013; 60.1% elsewhere in the paper). Carvalho et al. 2019, relaying WHO: 2016, ages 15 or older, men 8.6% (8.1–9.1), women 1.7% (1.6–1.9), total 5.1% (4.9–5.4); high-income countries 8.4% (8.0–8.9), upper-middle-income 5.4% (5.0–6.0).

evidence.extracted: NESARC-III interviewed 36,309 US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 or older face to face, April 2012 to June 2013, in households and selected group quarters; screener response 72.0%, person response 84.0%, total 60.1%; data weighted for oversampling and non-response and post-stratified to the 2012 American Community Survey. The authors state that homeless people, prisoners and most people in treatment are not covered, which may lead to underestimation.

evidence.extracted: The Introduction cites the 2013 National Survey on Drug Use and Health (SAMHSA) for a 12-month AUD prevalence of 7.0%. The Discussion reports that in that survey 12-month AUD stayed at about 7.5% from 2002 to 2013, against NESARC-III's DSM-IV 12.7% and its rise from 8.5% in 2001–2002, and says research on the discrepancies between national surveys is needed. The NSDUH itself was not read.

evidence.extracted: Definitions: a US standard drink is 14 g of pure alcohol; high-risk drinking is 4 or more drinks on any day for women or 5 or more for men, exceeded at least weekly in the past 12 months; DSM-IV AUD is 12-month abuse or dependence. Past-year DSM-IV AUD among people who drank in the past 12 months: 12.9% in 2001–2002 (interval printed as 12.3% to 17.5%, a misprint noted on the study card) and 17.5% (95% CI 16.7% to 18.3%) in 2012–2013; among people who drank at high risk: 46.5% (44.3% to 48.7%) and 54.5% (52.7% to 56.4%).

evidence.locator: Methods › Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › 12-Month DSM-IV AUD, 1st paragraph; Table 3; Methods › Assessments, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Past-year DSM-IV AUD was 8.5% (95% CI 8.0% to 8.9%) in the 2001–2002 NESARC (43,093 adults, response 81.0%) and 12.7% (12.1% to 13.3%) in the 2012–2013 NESARC-III (36,309 adults, response 60.0% in the Methods and 60.1% in the Limitations, with a $90 incentive); the paper gives the change only as a relative increase of 49.4%. The two surveys differed in sampling stages, approving bodies, incentive, census weighting base and instrument version; the only comparability check reported concerns three added abuse questions (8.5% against 8.2%; 12.7% against 12.2%). Editors' calculation: an absolute difference of 4.2 percentage points.

evidence.extracted: The Seminar relays, citing WHO's global status report, that alcohol use disorders affected 8.6% (95% CI 8.1–9.1) of men and 1.7% (1.6–1.9) of women aged 15 years and older in 2016, 5.1% (4.9–5.4) in all, highest in high-income (8.4%, 8.0–8.9) and upper-middle-income countries (5.4%, 5.0–6.0); the authors say these survey-based figures should be considered rough estimates because several criteria are culturally specific. The case definition behind the figures is not stated in the Seminar.

risk_of_bias.note: Study card sc_grant_2015 (JBI prevalence checklist), overall moderate: 60.1% response managed by weighting on a few characteristics; a household frame that leaves out homeless, imprisoned and most treated people, which the authors say biases the figure down; diagnosis by lay interviewers with fair-to-good agreement with clinicians (kappa 0.49 to 0.62). The change between the 2001–2002 and 2012–2013 surveys is rated high risk of bias on sc_grant_2017, which is why no trend is claimed.

inconsistency.note: Another national survey, as the same authors report it, gives about half the past-year figure (7.0% in 2013 and about 7.5% throughout 2002–2013, against 12.7% by DSM-IV and 13.9% by DSM-5 in NESARC-III); the surveys differ in instrument, sponsor and design, and the authors call for research on the discrepancy. The other survey was not read; its figure is taken as the authors give it.

indirectness.note: Worded for US household adults in 2012–2013 and the instrument used. The world figure is relayed second-hand and labelled so; the US figures do not depend on it.

imprecision.note: 36,309 respondents; standard error 0.31 points for the national past-year figure. Small subgroups are not cited.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable to a national survey.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (prevalence in survey populations): it starts low and is never upgraded. Rated down one level for risk of bias (response, frame and lay-interview diagnosis; JBI moderate on the card) and one for inconsistency (another national survey gives about half the past-year figure, unexplained), which reaches very low. The prevalence among people who drink (Grant et al., 2017) comes from the same 2012–2013 survey and is not independent of Grant et al. (2015). The rise from 2001–2002 to 2012–2013 is reported only with the reasons it cannot be read as a change in the population (sc_grant_2017: risk of bias high for the change; response 81.0% against about 60%; the other survey stable). The world figure comes from a narrative review relaying WHO (Carvalho et al., 2019), is second-hand and is not graded here. Status mixed: two US national surveys give inconsistent past-year figures, and no adequate explanation is offered.
